claim: Previous studies showed reorganised and/or altered activity in the primary sensorimotor cortex after a spinal cord injury (SCI).
source: Previous studies showed reorganised and/or altered activity in the primary sensorimotor cortex after a spinal cord injury (SCI), suggested to reflect abnormal processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: Somatotopic hand representations can be activated through attempted finger movements in the absence of sensory and motor hand functioning.
source: We found that somatotopic hand representations can be activated through attempted finger movements in the absence of sensory and motor hand functioning, and no spared spinal tissue bridges.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings from the fMRI study conducted on tetraplegic patients.

claim: Somatotopic hand representations can be activated in the absence of spared spinal tissue bridges.
source: We found that somatotopic hand representations can be activated through attempted finger movements in the absence of sensory and motor hand functioning, and no spared spinal tissue bridges.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural MRI data showing preserved somatotopy even without spared tissue bridges.

claim: Over years since SCI the hand representation somatotopy deteriorated.
source: However, over years since SCI the hand representation somatotopy deteriorated, suggesting that somatotopic hand representations are more easily targeted within the first years after SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis showing a negative relationship between time since injury and typicality of hand representations.

claim: Somatotopic hand representations are more easily targeted within the first years after SCI.
source: However, over years since SCI the hand representation somatotopy deteriorated, suggesting that somatotopic hand representations are more easily targeted within the first years after SCI.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that hand representation deteriorates over time.

claim: Following a tetraplegia, individuals mostly experience a loss of muscle function and sensation in their limbs and torso.
source: Following a tetraplegia (or cervical SCI), individuals mostly experience a loss of muscle function and sensation in their limbs and torso (Curt et al., 1998; Kalsi-Ryan et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) mostly receives weakened, or is fully deprived of, afferent inputs after tetraplegia.
source: Accordingly, the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) mostly receives weakened, or is fully deprived of, afferent inputs and is exposed to altered motor behaviour (Ozdemir and Perez, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The S1 hand area becomes largely unresponsive to tactile hand stimulation after chronic and complete cervical SCI in non-human primates.
source: Research in non-human primate models of chronic and complete cervical SCI has shown that the S1 hand area becomes largely unresponsive to tactile hand stimulation after the injury (Jain et al., 2008; Kambi et al., 2014; Liao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate studies.

claim: Surviving finger-related activity became disorganised after SCI in non-human primates such that a few somatotopically appropriate sites but also other somatotopically non-matched sites were activated.
source: The surviving finger-related activity became disorganised such that a few somatotopically appropriate sites but also other somatotopically non-matched sites were activated (Liao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific non-human primate study.

claim: SCI leads to extensive cortical reorganisation in S1 in non-human primates, such that tactile stimulation of cortically adjacent body parts activated the deprived brain territory.
source: Seminal non-human primate research has further demonstrated that SCI leads to extensive cortical reorganisation in S1, such that tactile stimulation of cortically adjacent body parts (e.g. of the face) activated the deprived brain territory (e.g. of the hand; Halder et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2008; Kambi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate research.

claim: The anatomical isomorphs of individual fingers are unchanged following chronic cervical SCI in non-human primates.
source: Although the physiological hand representation appears to largely be altered following a chronic cervical SCI in non-human primates, the anatomical isomorphs of individual fingers are unchanged (Jain et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a non-human primate study.

claim: A latent and somatotopic hand representation may be preserved regardless of large-scale physiological reorganisation after SCI.
source: This suggests that while a hand representation can no longer be activated through tactile stimulation after the disruption of afferent spinal pathways, a latent and somatotopic hand representation may be preserved regardless of large-scale physiological reorganisation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that anatomical isomorphs remain unchanged despite physiological changes.

claim: Representations of more impaired muscles retract or are absent while representations of less impaired muscles shift and expand after SCI in humans.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies induced current in localised areas of SCI patients' primary motor cortex (M1) to induce a peripheral muscle response. They found that representations of more impaired muscles retract or are absent while representations of less impaired muscles shift and expand (Fassett et al., 2018; Freund et al., 2011a; Levy et al., 1990; Streletz et al., 1995; Topka et al., 1991; Urbin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to TMS studies in human SCI patients.

claim: Cortically neighbouring body part representations can shift towards, though do not invade, the deprived M1 and S1 cortex after SCI in humans.
source: Similarly, human fMRI studies have shown that cortically neighbouring body part representations can shift towards, though do not invade, the deprived M1 and S1 cortex (Freund et al., 2011b; Henderson et al., 2011; Jutzeler et al., 2015; Wrigley et al., 2018; Wrigley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Attempted movements with the paralysed and sensory-deprived body part can still evoke signals in the sensorimotor system after SCI.
source: Other human fMRI studies hint at the possibility of latent somatotopic hand representations following SCI by showing that attempted movements with the paralysed and sensory-deprived body part can still evoke signals in the sensorimotor system (Cramer et al., 2005; Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Attempted movement activity levels have been shown to be increased after SCI.
source: This attempted 'net' movement activity was, however, shown to substantially differ from healthy controls: activity levels have been shown to be increased (Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018) or decreased (Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites (Freund et al., 2011b), and activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements (Cramer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Attempted movement activity levels have been shown to be decreased after SCI.
source: This attempted 'net' movement activity was, however, shown to substantially differ from healthy controls: activity levels have been shown to be increased (Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018) or decreased (Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites (Freund et al., 2011b), and activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements (Cramer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced during attempted movements after SCI.
source: This attempted 'net' movement activity was, however, shown to substantially differ from healthy controls: activity levels have been shown to be increased (Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018) or decreased (Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites (Freund et al., 2011b), and activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements (Cramer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites during attempted movements after SCI.
source: This attempted 'net' movement activity was, however, shown to substantially differ from healthy controls: activity levels have been shown to be increased (Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018) or decreased (Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites (Freund et al., 2011b), and activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements (Cramer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements after SCI.
source: This attempted 'net' movement activity was, however, shown to substantially differ from healthy controls: activity levels have been shown to be increased (Freund et al., 2011b; Kokotilo et al., 2009; Solstrand Dahlberg et al., 2018) or decreased (Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), volumes of activation have been shown to be reduced (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008), activation was found in somatotopically non-matched cortical sites (Freund et al., 2011b), and activation was poorly modulated when patients switched from attempted to imagined movements (Cramer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: Intracortical stimulation in the S1 hand area can elicit finger sensations in tetraplegic patients, hinting at preserved somatotopic representations.
source: Case studies using intracortical stimulation in the S1 hand area to elicit finger sensations in tetraplegic patients hint at such preserved somatotopic representations (Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016), with one exception (Armenta Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to case studies.

claim: One case study found negative results for intracortical stimulation eliciting finger sensations, suggested to be due to a loss of hand somatotopy and/or reorganisation in S1 or potential misplacement of the implant.
source: Case studies using intracortical stimulation in the S1 hand area to elicit finger sensations in tetraplegic patients hint at such preserved somatotopic representations (Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016), with one exception (Armenta Salas et al., 2018). Negative results were suggested to be due to a loss of hand somatotopy and/or reorganisation in S1 of the implanted tetraplegic patient, or due to potential misplacement of the implant (Armenta Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific case study.

claim: 14 chronic tetraplegic patients were tested with varying amounts of spared spinal cord tissue at the lesion level.
source: By measuring a group of 14 chronic tetraplegic patients with varying amounts of spared spinal cord tissue at the lesion level (quantified by means of midsagittal tissue bridges based on sagittal T2w scans), we uniquely assessed whether preserved connections between the brain and periphery are necessary to preserve fine somatotopic mapping in S1 (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study design and structural MRI measurements.

claim: A characteristic hand map shows a gradient of finger preference, progressing from the thumb (laterally) to the little finger (medially).
source: A characteristic hand map shows a gradient of finger preference, progressing from the thumb (laterally) to the little finger (medially).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of somatotopic organization.

claim: A characteristic progression of finger selective clusters was found in both the control and tetraplegic patient groups.
source: We found a characteristic progression of finger selective clusters in both the control and tetraplegic patient groups (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the traveling wave fMRI data and visualized in Figure 1.

claim: Inter-participant consistency was lowest for the little finger representation in both control and patient groups.
source: Qualitative inspection suggests that inter-participant consistency was lowest for the little finger representation in both groups.
evidence: This claim is based on qualitative inspection of the probability maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overall inter-participant consistency was reduced in the patient group compared to the control group.
source: It further appears that overall inter-participant consistency was reduced in the patient group compared to the control group.
evidence: This claim is based on qualitative inspection of the probability maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: Aspects of somatotopic finger selectivity were found in the maps of SCI patients' hands, similar to those observed in healthy controls.
source: Overall, we found aspects of somatotopic finger selectivity in the maps of SCI patients' hands, in which neighbouring clusters showed selectivity for neighbouring fingers in contralateral S1, similar to those observed in 18 age-, sex-, and handedness-matched healthy controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by individual finger selectivity maps shown in Figure 2.

claim: A characteristic hand map was found in a patient who suffered complete paralysis and sensory deprivation of the hands.
source: Notably, a characteristic hand map was even found in a patient who suffered complete paralysis and sensory deprivation of the hands (Figure 2B, patient map 1; patient S01).
evidence: This claim is supported by the finger selectivity map of patient S01 shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both controls and patients showed higher split-half consistency for comparison of the same fingers between two halves of the travelling wave dataset compared to neighbouring and non-neighbouring fingers.
source: Both controls and patients showed higher split-half consistency (assessed using the Dice overlap coefficient) for comparison of the same fingers between two halves of the travelling wave dataset (light blue), compared to neighbouring (blue), and non-neighbouring fingers (dark blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Dice overlap coefficient analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neighbouring fingers showed greater overlap across the split-halves of the dataset than non-neighbouring fingers for both patients and controls.
source: Moreover, neighbouring fingers showed greater overlap across the split-halves of the dataset then non-neighbouring fingers for both patients and controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Dice overlap coefficient analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overall, split-half consistency was not significantly different between patients and controls (F(1,20.32) = 0.51, p=0.48).
source: Overall, split-half consistency was not significantly different between patients and controls, as tested using a robust mixed ANOVA (see Figure 2C; F(1,20.32) = 0.51, p=0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Dice overlap coefficient data.

claim: There was a significant difference in split-half consistency between pairs of same, neighbouring, and non-neighbouring fingers (F(2,18.59) = 159.69, p<0.001).
source: There was a significant difference in split-half consistency between pairs of same, neighbouring, and non-neighbouring fingers (F(2,18.59) = 159.69, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Dice overlap coefficient data.

claim: The neighbourhood relationship in split-half consistency was not significantly different between the control and patient groups (F(2,18.59) = 2.44, p=0.11).
source: This neighbourhood relationship was not significantly different between the control and patient groups (i.e. there was no significant interaction; F(2,18.59) = 2.44, p=0.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the Dice overlap coefficient data.

claim: All patients were able to engage their S1 hand area by moving individual fingers (t(13) = 7.46, p<0.001; BF10 = 4.28 e + 3).
source: Overall, all patients were able to engage their S1 hand area by moving individual fingers (t(13) = 7.46, p<0.001; BF10 = 4.28 e + 3), as did controls (t(17) = 9.92, p<0.001; BF10 = 7.40 e + 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by univariate analysis of task-related activity in the S1 hand area.

claim: Controls were able to engage their S1 hand area by moving individual fingers (t(17) = 9.92, p<0.001; BF10 = 7.40 e + 5).
source: Overall, all patients were able to engage their S1 hand area by moving individual fingers (t(13) = 7.46, p<0.001; BF10 = 4.28 e + 3), as did controls (t(17) = 9.92, p<0.001; BF10 = 7.40 e + 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by univariate analysis of task-related activity in the S1 hand area.

claim: Patients' task-related activity in S1 was not significantly different from controls (t(30) = –0.82, p=0.42; BF10 = 0.44).
source: Furthermore, patients' task-related activity was not significantly different from controls (t(30) = –0.82, p=0.42; BF10 = 0.44), with the Bayes factor (BF) showing anecdotal evidence in favour of the null hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of task-related activity between groups.

claim: Inter-finger separability in the S1 hand area was greater than 0 for patients (t(13) = 9.83, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.77 e + 4).
source: We found that inter-finger separability in the S1 hand area was greater than 0 for patients (t(13) = 9.83, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.77 e + 4) and controls (t(17) = 11.70, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.92 e + 6), indicating that the S1 hand area in both groups contained information about individuated finger representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA analysis of the blocked design data.

claim: Inter-finger separability in the S1 hand area was greater than 0 for controls (t(17) = 11.70, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.92 e + 6).
source: We found that inter-finger separability in the S1 hand area was greater than 0 for patients (t(13) = 9.83, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.77 e + 4) and controls (t(17) = 11.70, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.92 e + 6), indicating that the S1 hand area in both groups contained information about individuated finger representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA analysis of the blocked design data.

claim: The S1 hand area in both groups contained information about individuated finger representations.
source: We found that inter-finger separability in the S1 hand area was greater than 0 for patients (t(13) = 9.83, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.77 e + 4) and controls (t(17) = 11.70, p<0.001; BF10 = 6.92 e + 6), indicating that the S1 hand area in both groups contained information about individuated finger representations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that inter-finger separability was greater than 0.

claim: For both controls and patients there was significantly greater separability in the S1 hand area than in a control CSF ROI.
source: Furthermore, for both controls (W = 171, p<0.001; BF10 = 4059) and patients (W = 105, p<0.001; BF10 = 279) there was significant greater separability (or representation strength) in the S1 hand area than in a control cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) ROI that would not be expected to contain information about individuated finger representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RSA results between S1 and CSF ROIs.

claim: There was no significant group difference in inter-finger separability of the S1 hand area (t(30) = 1.52, p=0.14; BF10 = 0.81).
source: We did not find a significant group difference in inter-finger separability of the S1 hand area (t(30) = 1.52, p=0.14; BF10 = 0.81), with the BF showing anecdotal evidence in favour of the null hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of inter-finger separability between groups.

claim: Inter-finger distances were not significantly different between patients and controls (F(1,21.66) = 1.50, p=0.23).
source: We did not find a significant difference in inter-finger distances between patients and controls (F(1,21.66) = 1.50, p=0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by robust mixed ANOVA analysis of inter-finger distances.

claim: Inter-finger distances were significantly different across finger pairs (F(9,15.38) = 27.22, p<0.001).
source: The inter-finger distances were significantly different across finger pairs, as would be expected based on somatotopic mapping (F(9,15.38) = 27.22, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by robust mixed ANOVA analysis of inter-finger distances.

claim: The pattern of inter-finger distances was not significantly different between groups (F(9,15.38) = 1.05, p=0.45).
source: This pattern of inter-finger distances was not significantly different between groups (i.e. no significant finger pair by group interaction; F(9,15.38) = 1.05, p=0.45).
evidence: This claim is supported by robust mixed ANOVA analysis of inter-finger distances.

claim: There was a significant difference in typicality between tetraplegic patients, healthy controls, and congenital one-handers (H(2) = 26.64, p<0.001).
source: We found a significant difference in typicality between tetraplegic patients, healthy controls, and congenital one-handers (H(2) = 26.64, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of typicality scores across groups.

claim: Controls had significantly higher typicality compared to congenital one-handers (U = 0, p<0.001; BF10 = 113.60).
source: As expected, post hoc tests revealed significantly higher typicality in controls compared to congenital one-handers (U = 0, p<0.001; BF10 = 113.60).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical tests comparing typicality scores.

claim: Inter-finger distances typicality of the SCI patients was significantly higher than the typicality scores of the congenital one-handers (U = 4, p<0.001; BF10 = 90.33).
source: Importantly, inter-finger distances typicality of the SCI patients was significantly higher than the typicality scores of the congenital one-handers (U = 4, p<0.001; BF10 = 90.33), but not significantly different from the typicality scores of the controls (U = 103, p=0.40; BF10 = 0.55).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical tests comparing typicality scores.

claim: Inter-finger distances typicality of the SCI patients was not significantly different from the typicality scores of the controls (U = 103, p=0.40; BF10 = 0.55).
source: Importantly, inter-finger distances typicality of the SCI patients was significantly higher than the typicality scores of the congenital one-handers (U = 4, p<0.001; BF10 = 90.33), but not significantly different from the typicality scores of the controls (U = 103, p=0.40; BF10 = 0.55).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical tests comparing typicality scores.

claim: The number of years since SCI significantly correlated with hand representation typicality (rs = –0.59, p=0.028).
source: We found that the number of years since SCI significantly correlated with hand representation typicality (see Figure 4A; rs = –0.59, p=0.028), suggesting that S1 hand representation typicality may deteriorate over time after SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Patients with more retained GRASSP motor function of the tested upper limb had more typical hand representations in S1 (rs = 0.60, p=0.02).
source: We further found that patients with more retained GRASSP motor function of the tested upper limb had more typical hand representations in S1 (see Figure 4B; rs = 0.60, p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and GRASSP sensory function of the tested upper limb (rs = 0.40, p=0.16).
source: We did not find a significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and GRASSP sensory function of the tested upper limb, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, or cross-sectional spinal cord area (see Figure 4C–E; rs = 0.40, p=0.16, rs = 0.46, p=0.14, and rs = 0.33, p=0.25, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level (rs = 0.46, p=0.14).
source: We did not find a significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and GRASSP sensory function of the tested upper limb, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, or cross-sectional spinal cord area (see Figure 4C–E; rs = 0.40, p=0.16, rs = 0.46, p=0.14, and rs = 0.33, p=0.25, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and cross-sectional spinal cord area (rs = 0.33, p=0.25).
source: We did not find a significant correlation between S1 hand representation typicality and GRASSP sensory function of the tested upper limb, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, or cross-sectional spinal cord area (see Figure 4C–E; rs = 0.40, p=0.16, rs = 0.46, p=0.14, and rs = 0.33, p=0.25, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Patients S01 and S03 did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level.
source: We further explored the hand representation typicality of patients S01 and S03 who did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, a complete (S01) or near complete (S03) hand paralysis, and a complete (S01) or near complete loss (S03) of hand sensory function (as assessed using the GRASSP test).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural MRI analysis of spinal tissue bridges.

claim: Patient S01 had complete hand paralysis.
source: We further explored the hand representation typicality of patients S01 and S03 who did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, a complete (S01) or near complete (S03) hand paralysis, and a complete (S01) or near complete loss (S03) of hand sensory function (as assessed using the GRASSP test).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASSP assessment data.

claim: Patient S03 had near complete hand paralysis.
source: We further explored the hand representation typicality of patients S01 and S03 who did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, a complete (S01) or near complete (S03) hand paralysis, and a complete (S01) or near complete loss (S03) of hand sensory function (as assessed using the GRASSP test).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASSP assessment data.

claim: Patient S01 had complete loss of hand sensory function.
source: We further explored the hand representation typicality of patients S01 and S03 who did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, a complete (S01) or near complete (S03) hand paralysis, and a complete (S01) or near complete loss (S03) of hand sensory function (as assessed using the GRASSP test).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASSP assessment data.

claim: Patient S03 had near complete loss of hand sensory function.
source: We further explored the hand representation typicality of patients S01 and S03 who did not have any spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, a complete (S01) or near complete (S03) hand paralysis, and a complete (S01) or near complete loss (S03) of hand sensory function (as assessed using the GRASSP test).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASSP assessment data.

claim: Both patients S01 and S03 had a highly typical hand representation in S1 that was significantly different from congenital one-handers.
source: Interestingly, both patients had a highly typical hand representation in S1 that was significantly different from congenital one-handers (i.e. who are born without a hand and do not have a missing hand representation; S01: t(12) = 3.20, p=0.008; S03: t(12) = 2.97, P = 0.01), but not controls (S01: t(17) = 0.95, p=0.36; S03: t(17) = 0.04, p=0.97).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of typicality scores.

claim: Both patients S01 and S03 had a highly typical hand representation in S1 that was not significantly different from controls.
source: Interestingly, both patients had a highly typical hand representation in S1 that was significantly different from congenital one-handers (i.e. who are born without a hand and do not have a missing hand representation; S01: t(12) = 3.20, p=0.008; S03: t(12) = 2.97, P = 0.01), but not controls (S01: t(17) = 0.95, p=0.36; S03: t(17) = 0.04, p=0.97).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of typicality scores.

claim: Retained connections between the periphery and the brain, retained motor functioning, and retained sensory functioning may not be necessary to maintain typical hand representations in S1.
source: This suggests that retained connections between the periphery and the brain, retained motor functioning, and retained sensory functioning may not be necessary to maintain typical hand representations in S1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the findings in patients S01 and S03.

claim: Years since SCI significantly predicted hand representation typicality in S1 with R2 = 0.40 (F(1,10) = 6.73, p=0.027).
source: Years since SCI significantly predicted hand representation typicality in S1 with R2 = 0.40 (F(1,10) = 6.73, p=0.027).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Motor function of the tested upper limb did not significantly add to the prediction of hand representation typicality (t = 1.43, p=0.19).
source: Motor function of the tested upper limb, sensory function of the tested hand, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, and spinal cord area did not significantly add to the prediction (t = 1.43, p=0.19, t = 1.44, p=0.18, t = 1.19, p=0.26, and t = 0.41, p=0.69, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Sensory function of the tested hand did not significantly add to the prediction of hand representation typicality (t = 1.44, p=0.18).
source: Motor function of the tested upper limb, sensory function of the tested hand, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, and spinal cord area did not significantly add to the prediction (t = 1.43, p=0.19, t = 1.44, p=0.18, t = 1.19, p=0.26, and t = 0.41, p=0.69, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level did not significantly add to the prediction of hand representation typicality (t = 1.19, p=0.26).
source: Motor function of the tested upper limb, sensory function of the tested hand, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, and spinal cord area did not significantly add to the prediction (t = 1.43, p=0.19, t = 1.44, p=0.18, t = 1.19, p=0.26, and t = 0.41, p=0.69, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Spinal cord area did not significantly add to the prediction of hand representation typicality (t = 0.41, p=0.69).
source: Motor function of the tested upper limb, sensory function of the tested hand, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level, and spinal cord area did not significantly add to the prediction (t = 1.43, p=0.19, t = 1.44, p=0.18, t = 1.19, p=0.26, and t = 0.41, p=0.69, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Some SCI patients' typicality scores fell in-between the able-bodied controls' and congenital one-handers' distributions.
source: While most tetraplegic patients' typicality scores fell in, or very close to, the able-bodied controls' distribution, we found that some SCI patients' typicality scores fell in-between the able-bodied controls' and congenital one-handers' distributions (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrapping analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Patients for whom most years had passed since their SCI had typicality scores that fell in-between the able-bodied controls' and congenital one-handers' distributions.
source: Interestingly, this included those patients for whom most years had passed since their SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by inspection of Figure 4F.

claim: S1 hand representations might deteriorate after an SCI, but some weak hand information may be maintained in S1 even >30 years after an SCI.
source: This suggests that S1 hand representations might deteriorate after an SCI, but some weak hand information may be maintained in S1 even >30 years after an SCI.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bootstrapping analysis and the observation that patients with longer time since injury still showed some hand representation.

claim: Detailed hand somatotopy can be preserved following tetraplegia, even in the absence of sensory and motor hand function and a lack of spared spinal tissue bridges.
source: Our results revealed that detailed hand somatotopy can be preserved following tetraplegia, even in the absence of sensory and motor hand function and a lack of spared spinal tissue bridges.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Over time since SCI finger maps deteriorated such that the hand somatotopy became less typical.
source: However, over time since SCI these finger maps deteriorated such that the hand somatotopy became less typical.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Spared spinal cord tissue bridges can be found in most patients with a clinically incomplete injury.
source: Spared spinal cord tissue bridges can be found in most patients with a clinically incomplete injury, their width being predictive of electrophysiological information flow, recovery of sensorimotor function, and neuropathic pain (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2021; Pfyffer et al., 2019; Vallotton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The width of spared spinal cord tissue bridges is predictive of electrophysiological information flow, recovery of sensorimotor function, and neuropathic pain.
source: Spared spinal cord tissue bridges can be found in most patients with a clinically incomplete injury, their width being predictive of electrophysiological information flow, recovery of sensorimotor function, and neuropathic pain (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2021; Pfyffer et al., 2019; Vallotton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level and sensorimotor hand function did not seem necessary to maintain and activate a somatotopic hand representation in S1.
source: However, in this study, spared midsagittal spinal tissue bridges at the lesion level and sensorimotor hand function did not seem necessary to maintain and activate a somatotopic hand representation in S1.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from patients S01 and S03.

claim: Time since injury was predictive of a deteriorated, or less typical, somatotopic S1 hand representation.
source: Time since injury was predictive of a deteriorated, or less typical, somatotopic S1 hand representation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Both patients S01 and S03 with typical S1 hand representations but absent spinal tissue bridges suffered their SCI only 4 years ago.
source: In fact, both patients with a typical S1 hand representations but absent spinal tissue bridges suffered their SCI only 4 years ago (the group was on average 12 years since SCI).
evidence: This claim is based on the demographic data of the patients.

claim: The hand representation typicality of patients who suffered their SCI further in the past were not similar to congenital one-handers' nor to controls' hand representation.
source: The hand representation typicality of patients who suffered their SCI further in the past were not similar to congenital one-handers' nor to controls' hand representation.
evidence: This claim is based on the bootstrapping analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Missing hand somatotopy is preserved even decades after arm amputation in amputees.
source: This finding complements previous studies in amputees showing that missing hand somatotopy is preserved even decades after arm amputation and that years since injury was not related to missing hand representation typicality (Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in amputees.

claim: Years since injury was not related to missing hand representation typicality in amputees.
source: This finding complements previous studies in amputees showing that missing hand somatotopy is preserved even decades after arm amputation and that years since injury was not related to missing hand representation typicality (Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in amputees.

claim: The injured axons within amputees' residual limb and the remaining part of the peripheral nerves mostly generate some spontaneous (ectopic) activity that is propagated to the brain.
source: The injured axons within amputees' residual limb and the remaining part of the peripheral nerves mostly generate some spontaneous (ectopic) activity that is propagated to the brain and could contribute to maintaining S1 representations (Kikkert et al., 2019; Kikkert et al., 2018; Kikkert et al., 2016; Makin et al., 2013; Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981; Vaso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spontaneous (ectopic) activity from injured axons could contribute to maintaining S1 representations in amputees.
source: The injured axons within amputees' residual limb and the remaining part of the peripheral nerves mostly generate some spontaneous (ectopic) activity that is propagated to the brain and could contribute to maintaining S1 representations (Kikkert et al., 2019; Kikkert et al., 2018; Kikkert et al., 2016; Makin et al., 2013; Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981; Vaso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and involves speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Amputees mostly remain able to move and receive afferents from the residual limb muscles that used to control the missing hand.
source: Furthermore, amputees mostly remain able to move and receive afferents from the residual limb muscles that used to control the missing hand as most of their motor system remains intact.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about amputation.

claim: Amputees' residual arm muscles are often still used either to move the residual limb and/or to control a prosthetic arm.
source: Although their hand is missing, amputees' residual arm muscles are often still used (either to move the residual limb and/or to control a prosthetic arm).
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about amputation and prosthetic use.

claim: Amputees' vividness of kinaesthetic sensations during phantom finger movements was found to be predictive of the typicality of the S1 missing hand representation.
source: Lastly, amputees' vividness of kinaesthetic sensations during phantom finger movements was found to be predictive of the typicality of the S1 missing hand representation (Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A continued, though altered, experience relating to the missing hand in amputees may contribute to maintaining the somatotopic missing hand representation in S1.
source: A continued, though altered, experience relating to the missing hand in amputees may contribute to maintaining the somatotopic missing hand representation in S1.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms maintaining representations in amputees.

claim: Tetraplegic patients mostly have reduced or a complete loss of communication between the brain and periphery.
source: Contrarily, tetraplegic patients mostly have reduced or a complete loss of communication between the brain and periphery.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about tetraplegia.

claim: Tetraplegic patients have problems activating the adequate muscles and will lose orderly afferents from their muscles and the skin.
source: They therefore have problems activating the adequate muscles and will lose orderly afferents from their muscles and the skin.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about tetraplegia.

claim: Continued disuse may cause somatotopic S1 representations to deteriorate after SCI.
source: It is possible that this continued disuse causes somatotopic S1 representations to deteriorate after SCI.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms of deterioration.

claim: S1 is reciprocally connected with various brain areas, for example, M1, lateral parietal cortex, posterior parietal area 5, secondary somatosensory cortex, and supplementary motor cortex.
source: S1 is reciprocally connected with various brain areas, for example,, M1, lateral parietal cortex, posterior parietal area 5, secondary somatosensory cortex, and supplementary motor cortex (Delhaye et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: After a loss of sensory inputs and paralysis through SCI, S1 representations may be activated and preserved through its interconnections with other brain areas.
source: After a loss of sensory inputs and paralysis through SCI, S1 representations may be activated and preserved through its interconnections with these areas.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms preserving representations.

claim: Cortico-cortical efference copies may keep a representation 'alive' through occasional corollary discharge.
source: Firstly, it is possible that cortico-cortical efference copies may keep a representation 'alive' through occasional corollary discharge (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This claim involves speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: When a motor command is initiated, an efference copy is thought to be sent to S1 in the form of corollary discharge.
source: When a motor command is initiated (e.g. in the form of an attempted hand movement), an efference copy is thought to be sent to S1 in the form of corollary discharge.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about motor control.

claim: Corollary discharge resembles the expected somatosensory feedback activity pattern and may drive somatotopic S1 activity even in the absence of ascending afferent signals from the hand.
source: This corollary discharge resembles the expected somatosensory feedback activity pattern and may drive somatotopic S1 activity even in the absence of ascending afferent signals from the hand (Adams et al., 2013; London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This claim involves speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attempting individual finger movements poses high attentional demands on tetraplegic patients.
source: Second, it is likely that attempting individual finger movements poses high attentional demands on tetraplegic patients.
evidence: This claim involves inference about the task demands.

claim: Attentional processes might have contributed to eliciting somatotopic S1 activity in tetraplegic patients.
source: Accordingly, attentional processes might have contributed to eliciting somatotopic S1 activity.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms.

claim: It is possible to activate somatotopic S1 hand representations through attending to individual fingers.
source: Evidence for this account comes from studies showing that it is possible to activate somatotopic S1 hand representations through attending to individual fingers (Puckett et al., 2017) or through touch observation (Kuehn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is possible to activate somatotopic S1 hand representations through touch observation.
source: Evidence for this account comes from studies showing that it is possible to activate somatotopic S1 hand representations through attending to individual fingers (Puckett et al., 2017) or through touch observation (Kuehn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attending to fingers during attempted finger movement task may have been sufficient to elicit somatotopic S1 activity through top-down processes in tetraplegic patients who lacked motor and sensory hand function.
source: Attending to fingers during our attempted finger movement task may have been sufficient to elicit somatotopic S1 activity through top-down processes in the tetraplegic patients who lacked motor and sensory hand function.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Observing others' or one's own fingers being touched or directing attention to others' hand movements or one's own fingers may help preserve somatotopic representations.
source: Furthermore, one might speculate that observing others' or one's own fingers being touched or directing attention to others' hand movements or one's own fingers may help preserve somatotopic representations.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about mechanisms.

claim: It is possible that somatotopic maps are relatively hardwired, and while they deteriorate over time, they never fully disappear.
source: Third, it is possible that these somatotopic maps are relatively hardwired, and while they deteriorate over time, they never fully disappear.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about the nature of somatotopic maps.

claim: Somatotopic mapping of a sensory-deprived body part has been shown to be resilient after dystonia.
source: Indeed, somatotopic mapping of a sensory-deprived body part has been shown to be resilient after dystonia (Ejaz et al., 2016; though see Burman et al., 2008 and Elbert et al., 1998) and arm amputation (Bruurmijn et al., 2017; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Somatotopic mapping of a sensory-deprived body part has been shown to be resilient after arm amputation.
source: Indeed, somatotopic mapping of a sensory-deprived body part has been shown to be resilient after dystonia (Ejaz et al., 2016; though see Burman et al., 2008 and Elbert et al., 1998) and arm amputation (Bruurmijn et al., 2017; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Even though a patient is clinically assessed to be complete and is unable to perceive sensory stimuli on the deprived body part, there may still be some ascending information flow that contributes to preserving somatotopy.
source: Fourth, it is possible that even though a patient is clinically assessed to be complete and is unable to perceive sensory stimuli on the deprived body part, there is still some ascending information flow that contributes to preserving somatotopy (Wrigley et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim involves speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: 48% of complete paraplegic SCI patients activated the location-appropriate S1 area in response to brushing stimulus on their toe, although they were unable to perceive the stimulus.
source: A recent study found that although complete paraplegic SCI patients were unable to perceive a brushing stimulus on their toe, 48% of patients activated the location-appropriate S1 area (Wrigley et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is unlikely that spinal tissue carrying somatotopically organised information would be missed by the assessment of spared spinal tissue bridges.
source: However, the authors of this study defined the completeness of patients' injuries via behavioural testing, while we additionally assessed the retained connections passing through the SCI directly via quantification of spared spinal tissue bridges through structural MRI. It is unlikely that spinal tissue carrying somatotopically organised information would be missed by our assessment (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the assessment method.

claim: Various processes may simultaneously influence the preservation of S1 somatotopy and elicit the observed somatotopic S1 activity.
source: Our experiment did not allow us to tease apart these potential processes, and it is likely that various processes simultaneously influence the preservation of S1 somatotopy and elicited the observed somatotopic S1 activity.
evidence: This claim involves inference about the complexity of mechanisms.

claim: Non-human primate studies demonstrated that remapping observed in S1 actually reflects reorganisation in subcortical areas of the somatosensory pathway, principally the brainstem.
source: Indeed, non-human primate studies demonstrated that remapping observed in S1 actually reflects reorganisation in subcortical areas of the somatosensory pathway, principally the brainstem (Chand and Jain, 2015; Kambi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to non-human primate research.

claim: The deprived S1 area receives reorganised somatosensory inputs upon tactile stimulation of neighbouring intact body parts.
source: As such, the deprived S1 area receives reorganised somatosensory inputs upon tactile stimulation of neighbouring intact body parts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited non-human primate research.

claim: Reorganisation and preservation of the original function could simultaneously occur within the same cortical area, allowing the original S1 representation of the deprived body part to be preserved.
source: This would simultaneously allow the original S1 representation of the deprived body part to be preserved, as observed in our results when we directly probed the deprived S1 hand area through attempted finger movements.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about how reorganization and preservation can coexist.

claim: In the first years after a tetraplegia the somatotopic S1 hand representation is preserved and can be activated through attempted movements even in the absence of retained sensory hand function, motor hand function, and spared spinal tissue bridges.
source: Together, our findings indicate that in the first years after a tetraplegia the somatotopic S1 hand representation is preserved and can be activated through attempted movements even in the absence of retained sensory hand function, motor hand function, and spared spinal tissue bridges.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Preserved S1 finger maps could be exploited in a functionally meaningful manner by rehabilitation approaches that aim to establish new functional connections between the brain and the hand after a tetraplegia.
source: These preserved S1 finger maps could be exploited in a functionally meaningful manner by rehabilitation approaches that aim to establish new functional connections between the brain and the hand after a tetraplegia, for example, through neuroprosthetic limbs or advanced exoskeletons that are directly controlled by the brain (Ajiboye et al., 2017; Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Bouton et al., 2016; Lebedev and Nicolelis, 2017).
evidence: This claim involves speculation about potential applications supported by citations.

claim: 15 chronic tetraplegic patients were recruited and 14 patients completed the measurements.
source: 15 chronic (i.e. > 6 months post injury) tetraplegic patients were recruited and 14 patients completed the measurements (mean age ± s.e.m. = 55 ± 3.6 years ; one female; six dominant left-handers; see Table 1 for demographic and clinical details).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample.

claim: The mean age of the 14 tetraplegic patients who completed measurements was 55 ± 3.6 years.
source: 15 chronic (i.e. > 6 months post injury) tetraplegic patients were recruited and 14 patients completed the measurements (mean age ± s.e.m. = 55 ± 3.6 years ; one female; six dominant left-handers; see Table 1 for demographic and clinical details).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample demographics.

claim: 18 age-, sex-, and handedness-matched able-bodied control participants participated in this study.
source: 18 age-, sex-, and handedness-matched able-bodied control participants (age = 56 ± 3.6 years; one female; five dominant left-handers) also participated in this study.
evidence: This claim describes the control group.

claim: Complete paraplegic patients are able to distinguish between attempted and imagined movements with their paralysed body part.
source: Importantly, complete paraplegic patients are able to distinguish between attempted and imagined movements with their paralysed body part (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008; Sabbah et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attempted foot movements activated SCI patients' motor network similarly to controls performing overt foot movements.
source: Furthermore, attempted foot movements activated SCI patients' motor network similarly to controls performing overt foot movements (Cramer et al., 2005; Hotz-Boendermaker et al., 2008; Sabbah et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RSA-based inter-finger distance patterns are thought to be shaped by daily life experience such that fingers used more frequently together in daily life have lower representational distances.
source: These inter-finger distance patterns are thought to be shaped by daily life experience such that fingers used more frequently together in daily life have lower representational distances (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RSA-based inter-finger distance patterns depict the invariant representational structure of fingers in S1 and M1 better than the size, shape, and exact location of the areas activated by finger movements.
source: RSA-based inter-finger distance patterns have been shown to depict the invariant representational structure of fingers in S1 and M1 better than the size, shape, and exact location of the areas activated by finger movements (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Congenital one-handers are born without a hand and therefore do not have a cortical representation of the missing hand.
source: Congenital one-handers are born without a hand and therefore do not have a cortical representation of the missing hand (unlike amputees who develop the representation before losing the hand and hence have a 'missing hand representation'; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Amputees develop the hand representation before losing the hand and hence have a 'missing hand representation'.
source: Congenital one-handers are born without a hand and therefore do not have a cortical representation of the missing hand (unlike amputees who develop the representation before losing the hand and hence have a 'missing hand representation'; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the sub-acute stage after SCI oedema and haemorrhage have largely resolved and hyperintense signal changes reliably reflect intramedullary neural damage.
source: It has been shown that already in the sub-acute stage after SCI oedema and haemorrhage have largely resolved and hyperintense signal changes reliably reflect intramedullary neural damage (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2019; Vallotton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High intra- and interobserver reliability has previously been reported for manual lesion segmentation at the lesion level using Jim 7.0 software.
source: We used Jim 7.0 software (Xinapse Systems, Aldwincle, UK) for manual lesion segmentation at the lesion level, for which high intra- and interobserver reliability has previously been reported (Huber et al., 2017; Pfyffer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.
